lebanese.notes: Beirut — heaviest French-Arabic-English code-switching of any Arab city. 'Bonjour habibti' is a real greeting.

syrian.notes: Damascus and Aleppo — more conservative phonology, melodic intonation.

jordanian.notes: Closer to Palestinian; bedouin influence in southern regions.

palestinian.notes: Strong oral tradition; closer to Jordanian; identity-laden.

casual_social.description: Default for Shami B2C social — warm, expressive, intimate-feeling.

professional_casual.description: Beirut LinkedIn / Amman B2B — French-English-Arabic blend in Lebanon.

grammar_quirks: Question word 'شو' (what) — distinct from Egyptian 'إيه' and Khaleeji 'وش'
Negation: 'ما' before verbs (ما بعرف = I don't know)
Future tense particle 'رح' or 'حـ' (رح روح = I'll go)
Lebanese: heavy French phonology influence in upper-class speech

code_switching_patterns.english_in_arabic: Heavy in Beirut, moderate in Amman, lighter in Damascus.
code_switching_patterns.french_in_arabic: Lebanese-specific — 'bonjour', 'merci', 'ça va' woven into casual conversation, especially among older generations and elite Beirut.
rules: Lebanese can mix Arabic + French + English in a single sentence — known as 'Lebanese trilingual'.
Syrian/Jordanian/Palestinian brands should keep French to zero unless explicitly Beirut-targeted.

beirut_lebanese: Trilingual blend, fashion-forward, melodic intonation, expressive
damascus_syrian: Warm, conservative, traditional respect markers, melodic

example_translations.english: Honestly, you have to try this.
example_translations.note: 'عنجد' is the natural Levantine intensifier. Avoid Egyptian 'بجد' or Khaleeji 'صدق'.
